content.title: About
content.content: Corn fritter is a crunchy snack made from whole corn kernels that are deep‑fried or air‑fried until golden. It has a light sweet corn flavor and a satisfying crisp texture. Fritters are commonly enjoyed as a snack, topping for salads, soups, or as a crunchy element in Asian dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn is one of the most widely cultivated crops worldwide, grown in over 150 countries.
Corn fritters originated in the United States in the early 20th century as a way to preserve surplus harvests.
Corn belongs to the grass family and is a close relative of sorghum, rice, and wheat.
There are several varieties of corn fritters: sweet, salted, spiced, and flavored with cheese or herbs.
Corn fritters are often used as a gluten‑free alternative to bread crumbs.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Corn provides fiber that supports healthy digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin in corn help protect the eyes from oxidative stress.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Fritters contain thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Provides magnesium and potassium
items.content: These minerals support muscle function, nerve signaling, and blood pressure regulation.

items.title: Low in fat when air‑fried
items.content: Compared with many fried snacks, air‑fried corn fritters contain relatively little fat.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Corn fritters can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Salted versions may contain significant amounts of sodium, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Potential acrylamide formation
items.content: Deep‑frying at very high temperatures can create acrylamide and other potentially harmful compounds.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Corn fritters can be enjoyed straight from the bag, tossed into salads, added to soups, used in tacos, or crushed as a crunchy coating for fish or chicken. They are convenient for on‑the‑go snacking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fritters in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For longer shelf life, store them in the refrigerator to prevent rancidity. Follow the expiration date printed on the package.

ham-prepackaged-or-deli-luncheon-meat-re.title: Ham, prepackaged or deli, luncheon meat, reduced sodium

content.title: About
content.content: Ham is cooked pork meat, often smoked, that is sold sliced. This version is formulated with reduced sodium (about 100 mg per 100 g), making it a better choice for those monitoring salt intake.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional ham is made from the hind leg of the pig, but other cuts can be used.
Reduced sodium is achieved by cutting back on salt during brining and using alternative flavor enhancers.
Ham is a common ingredient in sandwiches, salads, and snack platters.
In many countries ham is sold as deli‑style slices that can be stored in the fridge for several weeks.
Lower sodium content helps reduce the risk of elevated blood pressure.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Ham provides about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Reduced sodium
items.content: Less salt helps control blood pressure levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B12, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals contribute to immune function and DNA synthesis.

items.title: Convenient energy source
items.content: The combination of protein and modest fat provides quick, sustained energy.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Ham can contain moderate amounts of saturated fat, so people with high cholesterol should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some hams contain nitrites or other preservatives; choose additive‑free options if this is a concern.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: Rarely, individuals may have an allergic reaction to pork.

items.title: Shelf life after opening
items.content: Once opened, keep ham refrigerated and eat within 3–5 days.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Ham can be enjoyed sliced in sandwiches, added to salads, used in hot dishes such as pasta or omelets, or served as a snack alongside cheese and vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store ham in its original packaging or an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C. After opening, consume within a few days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

ice-cream-cone-soft-serve-vanilla.title: Ice Cream Cone, Soft Serve, Vanilla

content.title: About
content.content: Soft‑serve vanilla ice cream in a cone is a classic dessert made from cream, milk, sugar and natural vanilla extract. Served in a crisp waffle cone, it has a light, creamy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Soft‑serve ice cream originated in the United States in the 1930s and quickly became popular for its airy consistency.
Vanilla flavor is often derived from vanilla beans, but most commercial products use synthetic vanillin.
The waffle cone was invented in Italy in the early 1900s as a convenient way to hold ice cream.
Soft‑serve is served at about –6 °C, making it softer than traditional hard‑packed ice cream.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Dairy ingredients provide calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Milk and cream contain vitamins B2 and B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Lower fat content than regular ice cream
items.content: Soft‑serve is often made with reduced butterfat, resulting in fewer calories.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The product contains milk, so those with lactose intolerance should choose lactose‑free alternatives.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to casein or whey proteins.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Sweetness is achieved with added sugar, so consume in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Soft‑serve in a cone is best enjoyed straight from the machine. You can top it with sprinkles, fruit sauces, or nuts for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a freezer at –18 °C or lower. Once dispensed, soft‑serve loses its shape quickly, so it should be served immediately.

content.title: About
content.content: Kidney beans and brown rice are a classic combination of two whole foods, popular in vegetarian and vegan diets. Kidney beans provide plant protein and fiber, while brown rice supplies complex carbohydrates and B‑vitamins. Together they form a complete amino‑acid profile and deliver lasting satiety.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Kidney beans are a staple in Latin American cuisine and are known for their deep red color.
Brown rice retains the bran and germ, giving it more nutrients than white rice.
When paired, beans and rice create a “complete protein” containing all essential amino acids.
The soluble fiber in beans can help lower cholesterol levels.
Properly stored brown rice keeps its nutty aroma for up to six months.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Kidney beans deliver about 8 g of protein per 100 g, making them an excellent plant‑based protein source.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, helps regulate blood sugar, and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Brown rice releases glucose slowly, providing steady energy without spikes.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The duo supplies iron, magnesium, phosphorus, zinc, and B‑vitamins essential for metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Beans contain polyphenols, and brown rice provides ferulic acid, both of which combat free radicals.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Brown rice contains phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption; soaking or sprouting can mitigate this.

items.title: Hard‑to‑digest oligosaccharides
items.content: Beans have raffinose and stachyose, which may cause gas in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: A small percentage of people may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Toxin risk if undercooked
items.content: Kidney beans contain phytohemagglutinin, destroyed only by thorough boiling; undercooked beans can be toxic.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook beans and rice together as a pilaf, in soups, salads, or casseroles. Soak beans at least 8 hours, then boil them fully. Cook brown rice in a 1:2.5 ratio of rice to water for about 40‑45 minutes. Season with herbs, spices, and vegetables for variety.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry place for up to a year. Keep brown rice in a tightly sealed jar in the refrigerator to slow fat oxidation; it stays good for 6‑12 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Stewed rabbit, Puerto Rican style is a traditional dish from Puerto Rico made with tender rabbit meat simmered in a fragrant sauce of tomatoes, sweet peppers, garlic, onion, olive oil, and characteristic Puerto Rican spices such as adobo, oregano, and cumin. The dish has a rich, slightly sweet flavor with a gentle heat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: It is often served with rice, beans, and fried plantains.
In Puerto Rico rabbit is considered a leaner alternative to beef and pork.
The adobo sauce used in the recipe was introduced by Spanish colonists in the 16th century.
Rabbit meat is high in protein and low in fat, making it popular among athletes.
Traditional preparation uses earthenware pots, which enhance the aroma.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Rabbit meat provides about 21 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with many red meats, rabbit contains very little saturated fat, which is heart‑friendly.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish supplies vitamins B12, B3 and B6, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Rich in minerals
items.content: Rabbit provides iron, zinc and phosphorus, supporting immunity and bone health.

items.title: Antioxidant spices
items.content: Adobo seasoning and garlic are rich in antioxidants that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to rabbit meat.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Like any raw meat, rabbit can harbor salmonella or campylobacter; cook thoroughly to an internal temperature of 71 °C.

items.title: High sodium in sauce
items.content: Traditional adobo sauce can be salty; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Rabbit is relatively high in purines, which may aggravate gout in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the stewed rabbit hot, typically alongside boiled rice, beans, fried plantains, or corn bread. The meat can be shredded with a fork or cut into bite‑size pieces, and the sauce is used as a gravy.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the dish to room temperature, then place in an airtight container and refrigerate for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Thaw in the refrigerator and reheat until boiling.

content.title: About
content.content: Herbal hot tea is an infusion made from dried herbs, flowers, and spices, containing no caffeine. It is prepared by pouring boiling water over the plant material and steeping for several minutes. Herbal teas offer a wide range of aromas and flavors, from sweet and fruity to spicy and earthy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Herbal teas have been consumed in various cultures for over 5,000 years.
Unlike black or green tea, herbal infusions do not use Camellia sinensis leaves.
Some herbal teas, such as peppermint or chamomile, are traditionally used in folk medicine to relieve symptoms.
Herbal blends often combine several plants to achieve a desired taste and effect.
In some countries herbal teas are served in ceremonial contexts, for example, caffeine‑free infusions are offered during Japanese tea ceremonies.

items.title: Calms the nervous system
items.content: Herbs like chamomile, lavender, and lemon balm have mild sedative properties that help reduce stress and improve sleep.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Ginger, peppermint, and fennel promote digestive comfort, reducing bloating and nausea.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Plant components such as hibiscus and berry blends contain polyphenols that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Boosts immunity
items.content: Echinacea species are commonly used to support the immune system during colds.

items.title: Caffeine‑free
items.content: The absence of caffeine makes herbal teas suitable for children, pregnant women, and anyone avoiding stimulants.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some herbs (e.g., nettle or echinacea) may trigger allergies in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Herbal infusions such as St. John’s wort can affect the efficacy of medications, including antidepressants and birth control pills.

items.title: Pregnancy and breastfeeding
items.content: Certain herbs (e.g., sage, high‑dose peppermint) are not recommended during pregnancy.

items.title: Excessive consumption
items.content: Overuse of some herbs (e.g., licorice) can lead to high blood pressure or other imbalances.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Place 1‑2 teaspoons of dried herbal blend into 200‑250 ml of boiling water, cover, and steep for 5‑10 minutes. Strain and optionally add honey, lemon, or spices. Drink hot or chill for a refreshing summer beverage.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried herbs in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Keep moisture and direct sunlight away to preserve aroma and potency. Shelf life is typically 12‑24 months.
